findings.source_passage: and really will come to a settlement one of these days
findings.source_locator: After 'a mere bud on the forest tree of the parent suit'
findings.why_it_matters: This ironic coda is a classic Dickensian deadpan aside — the mock-reassurance that the suit 'really will come to a settlement one of these days' is a signature satirical beat that encapsulates the novel's whole critique of Chancery.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full sentence: 'For the question at issue is only a question of costs, a mere bud on the forest tree of the parent suit, and really will come to a settlement one of these days.'

findings.source_passage: some two or three of whom have inherited it from their fathers, who made a fortune by it
findings.source_locator: The 'solicitors in the cause' paragraph, describing the ranged solicitors
findings.why_it_matters: The clause 'who made a fortune by it' is interpretively essential: it exposes that the suit has enriched the legal profession while ruining its nominal parties, which is a central satirical thesis of the chapter.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'who made a fortune by it' after 'inherited it from their fathers.'

findings.source_passage: there are influences that can never come to good
findings.source_locator: In the 'How many people' paragraph, the 'In trickery, evasion' sentence
findings.why_it_matters: The source's formulation 'In trickery, evasion...there are influences that can never come to good' is a rhetorically shaped, generalized moral verdict; the draft's 'Trickery, evasion...never come to good' strips the rhetorical framing and weakens its voice.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore to: 'In trickery, evasion, procrastination, spoliation, botheration, under false pretences of all sorts, there are influences that can never come to good.'

findings.source_passage: Nothing can possibly come of the prisoner's conglomeration but his being sent back to prison, which is soon done. The man from Shropshire ventures another remonstrative 'My lord!'
findings.source_locator: Final scene, after the Chancellor speaks about the young people
findings.why_it_matters: The source's ironic commentary on the prisoner ('Nothing can possibly come of...') and the man from Shropshire's 'remonstrative' cry are character beats compressed away; the word 'remonstrative' and the deadpan verdict on the prisoner are signature voice moments.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore at minimum: 'Nothing can possibly come of the prisoner's conglomeration but his being sent back to prison, which is soon done. The man from Shropshire ventures another remonstrative "My lord!"'

summary: Three medium-severity losses — the ironic 'really will come to a settlement one of these days,' the damning 'who made a fortune by it,' and the flattened 'there are influences' formulation — collectively strip key satirical and interpretive beats from this signature chapter opening.
